title: A Freezer Multisig can remove a compromised Actor without disabling the role it acts through
content:
A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.2.5 defines a Revoker as an address on the AdministeredAgent "authorized to remove an Actor as a rapid-response measure, without affecting the Allocator Role held by the AdministeredAgent." The Freezer Multisig of a Prime Agent holds it, "providing the emergency capability to remove a compromised or malicious Actor outside the standard governance process."

Three properties make this a considered design rather than a convenience. First, the power is **strictly subtractive** — a Revoker can only remove; adding an Actor requires the separate Grantor role (A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.2.6). A compromised Freezer can cause denial of service but cannot authorize a single allocation.

Second, the intervention is **surgical**. Because the Allocator Role is held by the AdministeredAgent contract rather than by the operators themselves, revoking one Actor leaves the role, the Instance, and every other operator untouched. The alternative — revoking the Allocator Role — would halt all allocation activity to remove one bad key.

Third, it explicitly **bypasses governance timelocks**, conceding that key compromise moves faster than a governance vote. The safety argument for that bypass is precisely the asymmetry above: speed is granted only to the direction that cannot move funds.
description: The Revoker's power is subtractive-only and bypasses standard governance for speed;
